sections.title: What Is Git?
paragraphs: Git is a version control system that tracks changes to files over time. It is most often used for source code, but it can track almost any text-based project. Instead of saving files as final-v2-really-final.txt, Git stores a history of changes so you can see what changed, who changed it, and when it changed.
In practice, Git lets you work safely. You can experiment, undo mistakes, compare versions, and collaborate with other people without constantly copying folders by hand.
Tip: Think of Git as a timeline for your project. Every important save point becomes part of a history you can inspect and reuse later.

sections.title: Centralized vs Distributed Version Control
paragraphs: The biggest conceptual difference is between centralized and distributed systems.
In a centralized system, there is one main server with the official history. Developers check files in and out from that server.
Git is a distributed version control system. Every clone contains the full repository history, not just the latest files.
Note: Even though Git is distributed, teams usually still use a shared remote repository such as GitHub as the collaboration hub.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is Git and why is it used?

Git is a distributed version control system that records snapshots of a project over time, so you can see what changed, when, by whom and why, and return to any earlier state. It is used because it makes two otherwise hard things routine: several people editing the same codebase without overwriting each other, and experimenting on a branch without risking the working version. Every modern deployment pipeline is triggered by Git, which is why it is the one tool essentially every developer and operator shares.
What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

Git is the version control software that runs on your machine and does all the actual work. Committing, branching, merging, storing history. GitHub is a commercial website that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features Git does not have: pull requests, issues, code review, permissions and CI. Git works completely without GitHub, and GitLab, Bitbucket and self-hosted alternatives provide the same role. Confusing the two is common because most people meet Git through GitHub.
What does "distributed" mean in distributed version control?

Every clone is a complete repository, with the full history and every branch, rather than a thin checkout of a central server. That has three practical consequences: nearly every operation, log, diff, branch, commit, is local and therefore instant, you can work entirely offline and sync later, and there is no single point of failure because every clone is effectively a backup. Centralised systems such as SVN keep history only on the server, which is why they needed a connection for operations Git does in milliseconds.
Does Git store a copy of every file in every commit?

Conceptually yes. Each commit references a complete snapshot of the tree. Physically no: Git stores each unique piece of content once, addressed by its SHA-1 hash, so a file unchanged across a thousand commits is stored once and referenced a thousand times. It later repacks objects into compressed packfiles that store deltas between similar ones. This is why a repository with years of history is often smaller than the working directory it produced.
Do I need to know Git to work in DevOps?

Yes, and not merely to store code. Infrastructure as code, pipeline definitions, Kubernetes manifests and configuration all live in Git, and GitOps goes further by making the repository the declared desired state of production. That means a Git revert can be a rollback, a branch protection rule can be a deployment control, and a commit message can be the audit record for a change. Git fluency is closer to a prerequisite than a skill in this field.
What are the main Git terms a beginner needs?

Six carry most of the weight. A repository is the project plus its complete history. A commit is one recorded snapshot with a message and a parent. A branch is a movable pointer to a commit, which is why creating one is instant. HEAD is where you currently are. A remote is another copy of the repository, conventionally named origin. The staging area is the draft of your next commit, and it is the concept that makes the add-then-commit two-step make sense.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I check whether Git is already installed?

git --version prints the version if it is present. On macOS this can be misleading: the command may exist and trigger a prompt to install the Xcode Command Line Tools, or report an Apple-shipped build that lags well behind upstream. which git tells you where it came from, /usr/bin/git is Apple's, /opt/homebrew/bin/git or /usr/local/bin/git is Homebrew's. Install via Homebrew if you want current Git on a Mac.
What is the first thing to configure after installing Git?

Your identity, because Git refuses to commit without it and it is stamped permanently into every commit you make: git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "you@example.com". Use the email associated with your hosting account, or your commits will not be attributed to you. Then set init.defaultBranch main to match what GitHub and GitLab expect, and core.editor to something you can exit.
Why does Git say "Please tell me who you are"?

No user.name or user.email is configured, so Git cannot author a commit. Set them globally with the two --global commands, or per repository without the flag when a project needs a different address. The error usually appears on a brand new machine, or after cloning into a repository with a local config that cleared the values. Commits already made under the wrong identity can be corrected with git commit --amend --reset-author, though only safely before pushing.
Should I install Git with Homebrew or use the version macOS ships?

Homebrew, if you use Git seriously. The Apple-supplied build is tied to Xcode Command Line Tools updates and is often several minor versions behind, which means missing newer commands and flags, git switch and git restore arrived relatively recently, for example. brew install git gives you current Git that updates with everything else you have installed. Make sure Homebrew's path precedes /usr/bin in your PATH so the new one actually wins.
What is the difference between Git for Windows and Git in WSL?

They are two separate installations that do not share configuration or credentials. Git for Windows provides Git Bash and integrates with Windows tooling; Git inside a WSL distribution is a Linux Git operating on the Linux filesystem. Mixing them causes real problems, line endings, file permissions and credential helpers all differ, so pick one per project and stay with it. If you develop inside WSL, use WSL's Git and keep repositories in the Linux filesystem rather than under /mnt/c, which is also much faster.
How should I handle line endings across Windows, macOS and Linux?

Add a .gitattributes file to the repository with * text=auto so Git normalises text files to LF in history while checking them out natively, plus explicit rules for files that must stay LF, *.sh text eol=lf in particular, since a shell script with CRLF fails inside a Linux container with a baffling "not found". Committing .gitattributes is better than relying on each person's core.autocrlf setting, because it makes the behaviour a property of the project rather than of whoever cloned it.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between git add and git commit?

git add moves changes into the staging area, which is a draft of your next commit. git commit records whatever is staged as a permanent snapshot in history. The two-step design is the point: you can edit ten files and commit them as three logical commits by staging selectively, which makes history readable and reverting precise. git add -p takes this further, letting you stage individual chunks within a single file.
What is the difference between git init and git clone?

git init turns an existing directory into a new repository with no history and no remote. You use it once, when starting something from scratch. git clone <url> copies an existing remote repository, bringing its full history and automatically configuring origin so git push and git pull work immediately. If you init when you meant to clone, you end up with an empty repository and have to add the remote by hand with git remote add origin <url>.
How do I see what changed before committing?

git diff shows changes you have not staged, and git diff --staged shows what you have staged, that second one is the real pre-commit review, because it is exactly what the commit will contain. git status gives the file-level overview of both. A useful habit is git diff --staged immediately before every commit; it catches stray debug statements and accidentally staged files more reliably than any hook.
How do I unstage a file I added by mistake?

git restore --staged <file> removes it from the staging area while keeping your edits in the working directory. The older equivalent is git reset HEAD <file>, which you will still see in documentation and which does the same thing. If you want to discard the edits as well, git restore <file> does that, and it is not recoverable, since those changes were never recorded anywhere, so check git diff first.
What does git log show and how do I make it readable?

By default it prints every commit with full hash, author, date and message, which is a lot of screen for little information. git log --oneline gives one commit per line, and git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate adds the branch structure, which is the single most useful way to understand what state a repository is in. git log -p <file> shows the actual changes to one file over time, and git log --since="2 weeks ago" narrows the range.
Why does git commit open an editor, and how do I avoid it?

Because no message was supplied, so Git asks for one. Passing -m "your message" writes it inline and skips the editor, which is what most people use day to day. If the editor opens and you are stuck in Vim, :wq saves and :q! aborts the commit. Set something you know with git config --global core.editor "code --wait" for VS Code or "nano" for nano. Reserve the editor for commits that deserve a body explaining why, which -m makes awkward.

sections.title: What a Branch Really Is
paragraphs: A branch in Git is a movable pointer to a commit. Instead of copying your whole project into a new folder, Git lets you create a lightweight branch and continue work there.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between git switch and git checkout?

git checkout does several unrelated jobs, moving between branches, creating them, and restoring files, which made it a common source of accidents, since git checkout <file> silently discarded changes. Git split those responsibilities: git switch changes branches and git restore restores files. git switch -c <name> replaces git checkout -b <name>. Both new commands are stable and preferred in new work; checkout still functions and is not going away, so older documentation remains valid.
What does "detached HEAD" mean and how do I fix it?

HEAD normally points at a branch name, which in turn points at a commit. When you check out a commit, tag, or remote-tracking branch directly, HEAD points straight at that commit with no branch attached, that is detached. You can look around and even commit, but those commits belong to no branch and become unreachable once you leave. If you have made commits you want to keep, git switch -c <new-branch> right where you are captures them. If you have not, git switch main returns you to normal.
How do I delete a local and a remote branch?

git branch -d <name> deletes a local branch and refuses if it holds commits not merged anywhere, which is a safety net worth keeping; -D forces it. For the remote, git push origin --delete <name>. Deleting a remote branch does not remove other people's stale local copies of it. They need git fetch --prune, or git config --global fetch.prune true to have it happen automatically on every fetch.
How do I rename a Git branch?

git branch -m <new-name> renames the branch you are on, or git branch -m <old> <new> for another one. Renaming a branch that exists on the remote takes three steps, because the remote branch is a separate reference: rename locally, push the new name with git push origin -u <new-name>, then delete the old one with git push origin --delete <old-name>. Anyone else working on it needs to re-point their local branch, so agree the change first.
What is a good branch naming convention?

Use a short prefix that says what kind of change it is, then a brief description in kebab-case: feature/user-search, fix/login-redirect, chore/bump-deps. Many teams add the ticket number, feature/PROJ-412-user-search, which lets tooling link branches to issues automatically. Keep them lowercase and avoid spaces and unusual characters, since branch names become part of URLs and filesystem paths. The value is not aesthetic: a consistent scheme makes git branch --list 'fix/*' and automated cleanup possible.
Does creating a branch in Git copy all my files?

No, and this is why Git branching is fast where older systems were slow. A branch is a 41-byte file containing a commit hash. A pointer, nothing more. Creating one writes that file and does not touch your working directory at all, which is why git switch -c is instant even in a huge repository. Switching branches then updates only the files that actually differ between the two commits.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I resolve a Git merge conflict?

Open each file Git lists as conflicted and find the <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> markers. The section above ======= is the branch you are on, the section below is the branch you are merging in. Edit the file into the state you actually want, often a combination of both, not a choice between them, delete all three markers, then git add the file and git commit. git status tracks which files are still outstanding, and git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U lists just the unresolved ones.
What is the difference between a fast-forward and a three-way merge?

A fast-forward happens when the target branch has no commits since you branched off, so Git simply moves the pointer forward to your latest commit, no merge commit, and history stays linear. A three-way merge happens when both branches have moved on, so Git combines them using the common ancestor plus each tip, and records the result as a merge commit with two parents. You cannot choose: Git fast-forwards whenever it can, unless you pass --no-ff to force a merge commit.
When should I use git merge --no-ff?

When you want the branch to remain visible in history. --no-ff forces a merge commit even where a fast-forward was possible, so the graph shows that a group of commits belonged to one feature and git log --graph reads as a series of merged branches. That makes reverting a whole feature easy, one git revert -m 1 on the merge commit, and it is why many teams enable it for release branches. The cost is a busier graph, which is why other teams prefer squash merges instead.
How do I abort a merge and start over?

git merge --abort returns you to the state before the merge began, discarding partial resolutions. It works while the merge is in progress, that is, before you commit, which covers the case where the conflicts turn out to be more than you expected. If you have already committed the merge, use git reset --hard HEAD~1 to drop it locally, and git revert -m 1 <merge-sha> if it has already been pushed, since resetting a shared branch strands everyone else.
What does "Already up to date" mean when merging?

Every commit on the branch you are merging is already reachable from your current branch, so there is nothing to bring in. The usual cause is not having fetched: your local copy of the remote branch is stale, and Git is telling you the truth about what it knows. Run git fetch first, then merge. The other cause is merging the wrong direction. Merging main into your feature branch when you meant to merge your feature into main.
Should my team use merge commits, squash merges, or rebase merges?

Squash merges suit most teams: each pull request becomes one commit on main, so history reads as a list of shipped changes and reverting is trivial, at the cost of losing the individual commits. Merge commits preserve everything and keep the branch visible, which matters when you need the full record for audit or bisecting inside a feature. Rebase merges give a linear history with every commit kept, which is tidy but rewrites hashes. Pick one and enforce it in the repository settings rather than leaving it per-developer.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between git rebase and git merge?

Both integrate one branch into another; they differ in what history they leave behind. git merge creates a merge commit joining the two lines of development, preserving exactly what happened including the fact that work happened in parallel. git rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, producing a straight line as though you had started from the latest code. Merge is honest about history and clutters the graph; rebase is tidy and rewrites commit hashes. Most teams rebase local feature branches before opening a pull request, then merge the result.
Is it safe to rebase a branch that has been pushed?

Only if you are the only person working on it. Rebasing creates new commits with new hashes, so the remote branch and your local one diverge and git push is rejected until you force it. Use git push --force-with-lease rather than --force: it refuses the push if someone else has added commits you have not seen, which turns silent data loss into an error message. Never rebase a shared branch such as main. Everyone who has pulled it will be stranded on commits that no longer exist.
How do I squash multiple commits into one?

Run git rebase -i HEAD~n where n is how many commits back you want to go, then change pick to squash (or s) on every commit except the first. The first stays pick because the others are folded into it. Git then opens an editor to combine the messages. If you only want the first commit's message, use fixup instead of squash to discard the others. Many platforms also offer "Squash and merge" on a pull request, which achieves the same result without rebasing locally.
How do I get out of a rebase that has gone wrong?

git rebase --abort returns the branch to exactly where it was before the rebase started, at any point during the process. That is the escape hatch to reach for whenever you are unsure. If the rebase has already completed and you want the old state back, git reflog lists where HEAD has been, and git reset --hard HEAD@{n} moves you to the entry before the rebase. The reflog is why a completed rebase is recoverable and why "I lost my work" is almost never actually true.
Why do I keep hitting the same conflict repeatedly during a rebase?

Because a rebase replays each commit in turn, so a line you changed in several commits conflicts once per commit. Resolve the file, git add it, then git rebase --continue to move to the next one. Two things help: squashing related commits before rebasing so there are fewer replays, and enabling git config --global rerere.enabled true, which records how you resolved a conflict and reapplies that resolution automatically the next time the identical conflict appears.
What does git pull --rebase do and should I use it?

It fetches the remote branch and replays your local commits on top of it, instead of creating a merge commit. Without it, a plain git pull on a branch that has moved on both sides produces a "Merge branch 'main' of ..." commit, and a busy repository fills with them. Setting git config --global pull.rebase true makes it the default and keeps history linear. It is safe for your own unpushed commits, which is exactly what git pull is dealing with.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?

git fetch downloads commits and updates your remote-tracking branches such as origin/main, and changes nothing in your working directory. It is always safe to run. git pull is fetch followed immediately by a merge (or rebase) into your current branch, so it does alter your files and can produce conflicts. The useful habit is git fetch then git log origin/main..main to see what diverged before deciding how to integrate it, rather than letting pull decide for you.
How do I fix "rejected, non-fast-forward" when pushing?

The remote branch has commits you do not have locally, so accepting your push would discard them. Run git pull --rebase to replay your work on top of theirs, resolve any conflicts, then push. Do not reach for git push --force, which deletes their commits. If you genuinely must overwrite, after an intentional rebase of your own feature branch, use git push --force-with-lease, which refuses the push if the remote has moved since you last fetched.
What does git push -u origin main actually do?

-u (short for --set-upstream) records origin/main as the upstream of your local main, in addition to pushing. That association is what lets you type bare git push, git pull and git status afterwards and have Git know which remote branch you mean, including the "your branch is ahead by 2 commits" line in git status. You need it once per branch; after that the plain commands work. git branch -vv shows which branches have an upstream set.
Why don't I see a colleague's new branch?

Your local copy of the remote's branch list is only updated when you fetch. Run git fetch (or git fetch --all for every remote) and then git branch -r lists the remote branches you know about. The reverse problem is stale entries for branches that have been deleted upstream, which git fetch --prune clears; git config --global fetch.prune true makes that automatic on every fetch.
What is the difference between origin and upstream?

They are just remote names, not Git concepts. origin is the conventional name for the repository you cloned from, set automatically by git clone. upstream is the convention in fork-based workflows for the original project you forked: origin is your fork and upstream is the source. That is what makes git fetch upstream && git rebase upstream/main the standard way to bring a fork up to date. Add it with git remote add upstream <url>, and git remote -v lists what you have.
How do I change a remote's URL, for example from HTTPS to SSH?

git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git, then confirm with git remote -v. This is the usual fix when HTTPS pushes start asking for a password that no longer works. GitHub stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations, so HTTPS needs a personal access token while SSH uses your key. Switching to SSH avoids the credential prompt entirely once your key is added to the account.

paragraphs: What is the difference between git stash apply and git stash pop?

Both restore the stashed changes to your working directory. pop then deletes the stash entry; apply leaves it in the list. Use apply when you want to put the same work onto more than one branch, or when you are not yet sure the restore will go cleanly, if it conflicts badly you still have the stash to fall back on. No, and this surprises people regularly. A plain git stash leaves new files sitting in your working directory, so switching branches carries them along and a "clean" stash turns out not to be. Use git stash -u (or --include-untracked) to include them, and git stash -a (--all) to include ignored files as well. Because -a sweeps up build output and node_modules, it is rarely what you want.
How do I see what is in a stash before restoring it?

git stash list shows the entries with their references. git stash show stash@{0} gives a summary of changed files, and git stash show -p stash@{0} prints the full diff. You can also restore a single file from a stash without applying the whole thing: git checkout stash@{0} -- path/to/file. Naming stashes as you create them, git stash push -m "half-done search filter", makes the list readable a week later, which the default WIP on main messages do not.
I dropped a stash by accident. Can I recover it?

Usually yes. A dropped stash is an unreachable commit, and git fsck --unreachable | grep commit lists candidates you can inspect with git show <sha>. Once you find it, git stash apply <sha> restores the contents. It works until Git garbage-collects, which is typically not for weeks. The wider lesson is that stashes are the least durable place to keep work. A throwaway commit on a scratch branch is recoverable through the reflog and cannot be dropped by a stray git stash clear.
How do I apply a stash to a different branch?

Just switch branches and apply it. Stashes are not tied to the branch they were created on. git switch other-branch then git stash pop is a standard way to move work you started in the wrong place. Conflicts are possible if the branches have diverged in the same files, and git checkout --theirs/--ours plus normal conflict resolution applies. If you expect trouble, use apply rather than pop so the stash survives a failed attempt.
When should I use a branch instead of a stash?

Whenever the work will outlive the next half hour. A stash is an unnamed, unordered pile that is easy to forget and easy to clear, and git stash list after a busy fortnight is nobody's friend. For anything you intend to return to, commit it on a branch, even as a scrappy "wip" commit you later amend or squash. Stash is at its best for exactly what it was designed for: parking a few minutes of work to pull, switch branch for a quick fix, or check something on a clean tree.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between git reset and git revert?

git reset moves the branch pointer backwards, rewriting history so the commits are no longer on the branch. git revert leaves history intact and creates a new commit that applies the inverse of an old one. The distinction is about who else has the commits: reset is right for local work nobody has pulled, and revert is the only safe choice on a shared branch, because resetting a pushed branch strands everyone who already fetched those commits. On main, always revert.
How do I undo my last commit but keep the changes?

git reset --soft HEAD~1 moves the branch back one commit and leaves everything staged, ready to recommit, which is what you want when you simply mis-worded the message or forgot a file. git reset HEAD~1 (mixed, the default) does the same but unstages the changes, leaving them in your working directory. Use git commit --amend instead if you only want to fix the message or add a file to the commit that is already there, since it avoids the reset entirely.
What is the difference between git reset --soft, --mixed and --hard?

All three move HEAD; they differ in how much they touch. --soft moves the pointer only, leaving your staging area and files exactly as they were, so the undone changes are staged. --mixed, the default, also resets the staging area, so the changes sit unstaged in your working directory. --hard resets the working directory too, discarding the changes completely. Only --hard destroys work, which is why it is the one to pause over.
I ran git reset --hard and lost my work. Can I get it back?

Committed work, yes. git reflog lists every position HEAD has held, including the commit you reset away from, and git reset --hard HEAD@{1} puts you back. Reflog entries persist for about 90 days by default, so recovery is realistic long after the mistake. Work that was never committed is genuinely gone, --hard overwrites the working directory and there is no record of it. That asymmetry is the strongest argument for committing early and often, even on messy work-in-progress.
How do I discard changes to a single file?

git restore <file> discards unstaged changes in that file, and git restore --staged <file> unstages it while keeping the edits. Those two replace the overloaded git checkout -- <file> and git reset HEAD <file> forms, which did the same jobs less clearly. To do both, unstage and discard, use git restore --staged --worktree <file>. Discarding is not recoverable, since the changes were never recorded anywhere, so check git diff before running it.
How do I remove untracked files and directories?

git clean -fd deletes untracked files and directories, with -f required because Git refuses to do something this destructive without it, and -d extending it to directories. Always run git clean -nd first: -n is a dry run that lists exactly what would be removed. By default .gitignored files are left alone, and -x includes them. Useful for wiping build output and node_modules, and a fast way to delete a local .env you meant to keep.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between a lightweight and an annotated Git tag?

A lightweight tag is just a name pointing at a commit. Nothing else is stored. An annotated tag is a real Git object with a tagger, a date, a message and optionally a GPG signature. That difference matters in practice: git describe only considers annotated tags by default, and you cannot tell who created a lightweight tag or why. Use annotated tags (git tag -a v1.2.0 -m "...") for anything released, and lightweight tags for private bookmarks.
Why don't my tags appear on GitHub after pushing?

Because git push does not include tags. Push one with git push origin v1.2.0, or all of them with git push origin --tags. If you want annotated tags pushed along with commits automatically, git push --follow-tags sends the annotated tags that are reachable from the commits being pushed, which is usually the behaviour people expect, and is worth setting as a habit for release work.
How do I delete a Git tag locally and remotely?

git tag -d v1.2.0 removes it locally, and git push origin --delete v1.2.0 removes it from the remote. Be careful with released tags: anyone who has already fetched keeps their copy, and if your release tooling or a package registry resolved that tag, deleting it can break builds that referenced it. The safer convention for a bad release is to publish a new tag rather than to remove the old one.
Can I tag a commit from the past?

Yes. Pass the commit hash: git tag -a v1.0.0 9fceb02 -m "Initial release". The tag's own date is when you created it, not the commit's date, which occasionally matters for tooling that sorts by tag date. This is the usual way to add a version tag retrospectively when a project started without them, and git log --oneline gives you the hashes to work from.
What happens when I check out a tag?

You get a detached HEAD, because a tag points at a fixed commit rather than a moving branch. That is fine for inspecting or building a release. If you need to make changes, a hotfix on an old version, create a branch from it: git switch -c hotfix/1.2.1 v1.2.0. Committing while detached produces commits that belong to no branch and become unreachable once you switch away.
How do tags relate to releases and semantic versioning?

A tag is the Git primitive; a "release" on GitHub or GitLab is a layer on top of a tag, adding notes and downloadable artefacts. The convention is a v prefix and semantic versioning, v1.4.2, where the major number changes on a breaking change, the minor on a backwards-compatible feature, and the patch on a fix. Most release automation, including semantic-release, works by reading commits since the last tag and creating the next one, so consistent tagging is what makes the automation possible.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between forking and cloning?

Cloning copies a repository to your machine; forking copies it to your own account on the hosting platform, and you then clone your fork. You clone when you have write access to the original. The normal case inside a company. You fork when you do not, which is how open-source contribution works: you push branches to your fork and open a pull request across repositories. In a fork workflow, origin is your fork and upstream is the original project.
How do I keep my branch up to date with main?

git fetch origin then either git rebase origin/main for a linear history or git merge origin/main to keep a merge commit. Rebase is the usual choice on your own feature branch before review, since it makes the pull request read as though written against current code. Remember it needs git push --force-with-lease afterwards, because the hashes change. Merge is the right choice if others are working on the same branch, as rebasing shared work strands them.
What is the difference between squash, merge and rebase merge on a pull request?

Squash merge collapses every commit in the branch into one on main. The tidiest history and the easiest to revert, at the cost of losing the individual commits. Merge commit keeps all commits and adds one joining them, preserving the full record and showing the branch in the graph. Rebase merge replays each commit onto main individually, giving a linear history that keeps them all but rewrites their hashes. Pick one, set it in repository settings, and stop thinking about it.
How big should a pull request be?

Small enough to review properly in one sitting. A few hundred changed lines is a reasonable ceiling. Review quality falls off sharply beyond that, and a large pull request tends to receive approval rather than scrutiny, which is the opposite of the point. If a change is genuinely large, split it: a mechanical refactor as one pull request, the behaviour change as another. Separating a rename or reformat from real logic changes is the single most effective thing you can do for reviewability.
Should I force-push to a pull request branch?

It is fine and often necessary, after a rebase onto main, or after squashing review fixes, provided you use git push --force-with-lease, which refuses if the remote has commits you have not fetched. What it costs is review continuity: a force-push can detach existing review comments from the lines they referred to. A common compromise is to add plain commits during review so reviewers can follow the changes, then squash on merge.
What should I actually look for when reviewing code?

Correctness first, then whether the change is understandable without the author present, then tests covering the behaviour rather than the implementation. Leave formatting to a linter. A review that spends its attention on spacing has spent it on the thing a tool should have handled. Be specific and direct about problems, ask rather than assert when you may have missed context, and distinguish blocking concerns from suggestions so the author knows what actually needs to change.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What does git cherry-pick do?

It applies the changes from one commit onto your current branch as a new commit with a new hash. The classic use is a hotfix: the fix is committed on main and you need the same change on a release branch without bringing everything else along. git cherry-pick <sha> does it; -x appends a line recording the original hash, which is worth using so the duplication is traceable. Cherry-picking the same change into two branches that later merge can produce a conflict, which is the main reason to prefer merging where you can.
How does git bisect find a bug?

By binary search through history. You tell it a commit where the bug exists (git bisect bad) and one where it does not (git bisect good), and it checks out the midpoint for you to test, narrowing by half each round, around ten steps for a thousand commits. Mark each as good or bad and it names the first bad commit. git bisect run ./test.sh automates it entirely when you have a script that exits non-zero on failure, which turns an afternoon of guessing into a couple of minutes.
What is git reflog and when does it save you?

The reflog records every position HEAD has held in your local repository, including states no branch points at any more. That makes it the recovery tool for a bad reset --hard, a rebase that went wrong, a deleted branch, or a commit you amended away: git reflog lists the history, then git reset --hard HEAD@{5} or git switch -c recovered <sha> brings it back. Entries last about 90 days by default. It is local only, which is why committing is the real safety net.
What is the difference between git cherry-pick and git rebase?

Rebase replays a whole series of commits onto a new base; cherry-pick applies one or a few chosen commits. Under the surface they do much the same work, rebase is essentially a scripted sequence of cherry-picks, so the choice is about scope. Rebase for "move my branch on top of the latest main", cherry-pick for "I need just that one fix over here".
How do I find which commit introduced a specific line?

git blame <file> annotates every line with the commit, author and date that last changed it, and git blame -L 40,60 <file> limits it to a range. When blame only shows a formatting commit, git blame -w --ignore-rev <sha> skips whitespace changes and a specified reformat. For searching by content rather than location, git log -S "functionName" finds commits where the number of occurrences of that string changed, which is the fastest way to locate when something was added or deleted.
Which advanced Git commands are actually worth learning first?

Three, in this order. git reflog, because it turns most disasters into inconveniences and takes five minutes to understand. git bisect, because nothing else finds a regression in a long history nearly as fast. And git log -S, because "when did this string appear" is a question you ask constantly. Cherry-pick and interactive rebase are valuable but situational, and submodules are best avoided until you have a specific need for them.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What are Git hooks and where do they live?

Hooks are executable scripts Git runs automatically at points in its workflow. Before a commit is created, after a message is written, before a push. They live in .git/hooks, which ships with .sample files you can rename to activate. The crucial consequence of that location is that .git is not version-controlled, so a hook you write is yours alone: it does not travel with a clone and nobody else on the team gets it.
Why don't my Git hooks work for the rest of the team?

Because .git/hooks is outside the repository's tracked content, so hooks are never committed, pushed or cloned. Every developer would have to create them by hand, and nothing keeps them in sync. The standard fix is a manager such as Husky or pre-commit, which stores hook definitions in tracked files and points Git's core.hooksPath at a committed directory during install, so a fresh clone plus npm install sets everything up.
What is the difference between client-side and server-side hooks?

Client-side hooks run on a developer's machine, pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push, and are about fast feedback: catching a lint error in two seconds rather than two minutes of CI. Server-side hooks such as pre-receive and update run on the remote when a push arrives, and are about enforcement, because they cannot be skipped. Hosted platforms generally do not expose server-side hooks; branch protection rules and required status checks fill that role instead.
Can Git hooks be bypassed?

Yes, trivially, git commit --no-verify skips pre-commit and commit-msg, and git push --no-verify skips pre-push. That is a feature, since you sometimes need to commit through a broken hook, but it means client-side hooks are a convenience and not a control. Anything that genuinely must hold has to be checked where the developer cannot reach it: a required CI check on a pull request, or a server-side hook on self-hosted infrastructure.
What should I put in a pre-commit hook?

Only fast checks, and preferably only on the files being committed. Formatting and linting staged files is the classic use, lint-staged exists specifically for this, plus a scan for accidentally committed secrets. Keep it under a couple of seconds: a pre-commit hook that runs the full test suite gets disabled by the team within a week, and rightly so. Put the slow, comprehensive checks in CI, where they belong.
How do I set up Husky for a JavaScript project?

Install it as a dev dependency, run npx husky init, and it creates a .husky directory and a prepare script so the hooks install automatically after npm install. Add a hook by writing the command into .husky/pre-commit, commonly npx lint-staged, and commit that file. Because .husky is tracked, everyone gets the same hooks on their next install, which is the whole problem raw .git/hooks cannot solve.

A larger organization with formal release windows often prefers GitFlow.

sections.title: What You Should Remember
paragraphs: GitFlow adds structure for releases and hotfixes, GitHub Flow keeps things simple around main and pull requests, and Trunk-Based Development pushes toward very fast integration with short-lived branches and feature flags. The best workflow is the one that matches your release cadence, team size, and automation maturity.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between GitFlow, GitHub Flow and trunk-based development?

They differ in how many long-lived branches exist. GitFlow keeps main, develop, plus release and hotfix branches. Heavy, but it models versioned software with several supported releases. GitHub Flow keeps only main plus short-lived feature branches, each merged via pull request and deployed on merge. Trunk-based development goes furthest: everyone commits to main at least daily, with incomplete work hidden behind feature flags rather than branches. The trade is branch isolation against integration pain. The longer a branch lives, the worse its merge.
Which Git workflow should a small team use?

GitHub Flow, in almost every case. One protected main, a short-lived branch per change, a pull request for review, deploy on merge. It is enough process to keep main releasable and little enough that nobody spends time on branch bookkeeping. GitFlow's develop and release branches only pay off when you genuinely maintain multiple versions in production simultaneously, and adopting it without that need is the most common case of a workflow costing more than it returns.
Is GitFlow still recommended?

Only for software with real release management. Desktop applications, on-premise products, anything where several versions are supported at once and hotfixes must land on old releases. Its author has said as much: for continuously deployed web services the extra branches add ceremony without benefit. If you deploy from main several times a week, GitHub Flow or trunk-based development fits the reality better, and the release branch you are maintaining is usually just a delay.
What are feature flags and why does trunk-based development need them?

A feature flag is a runtime switch that decides whether new code paths are active, letting you merge unfinished work into main safely because it is simply off. Trunk-based development depends on them: if everyone integrates daily, there is no long branch in which to hide an incomplete feature, so the hiding has to move into the code. The cost is real, flags accumulate, and each one doubles the possible states, so removing them once a feature ships has to be part of the process.
How long should a feature branch live?

A day or two; a week at the outside. Merge difficulty grows with the square of the time, roughly, because both your branch and main keep moving and the overlap compounds. If a change cannot be finished in that window, split it into separately shippable pieces, a refactor, then the behaviour behind a flag, rather than letting the branch run. "Long-lived feature branch" is close to a synonym for "painful merge".
How do branch protection rules fit into a workflow?

They are what makes the workflow actually happen rather than being a document people mean to follow. On main, typical rules require a pull request rather than a direct push, at least one approving review, passing status checks, and an up-to-date branch before merge. Setting the merge strategy, squash, merge commit or rebase, at the repository level is worth doing too, since leaving it per-developer produces a history with all three. Enforce it centrally; local hooks can be bypassed with --no-verify.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: Where is my .gitconfig file and what are the config scopes?

There are three, each overriding the one above. System config applies to every user on the machine (/etc/gitconfig, edited with --system). Global config is yours (~/.gitconfig, edited with --global) and is where nearly everything belongs. Local config belongs to one repository (.git/config, the default with no flag) and is what you use to override your identity for a single project. git config --list --show-origin prints every setting alongside the file it came from, which settles most "why is this value set" questions.
How do I use a different email for work and personal repositories?

Set the work identity per repository with git config user.email you@company.com, which writes to that repository's .git/config and overrides your global value. For more than a couple of repositories, use conditional includes: in ~/.gitconfig, an [includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"] section pointing at a second config file applies automatically to anything under that directory. That way a new clone in the right folder gets the right identity without you remembering to set it.
How do I create a Git alias?

git config --global alias.<name> '<command>', so git config --global alias.st status gives you git st. Aliases can chain flags, as with a pretty log: alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate --all". Prefixing the value with ! runs a shell command rather than a Git subcommand, which lets an alias combine several steps. Aliases live in your config, so they are yours alone and do not travel with the repository.
Which Git aliases are actually worth setting up?

Start with the ones you type dozens of times a day, st for status, co for checkout or switch, br for branch, ci for commit. Then add the ones whose full form you would never type: a graph log, last for log -1 HEAD, and unstage for restore --staged. Do not alias destructive commands to short names; a two-character alias for reset --hard is an accident waiting to happen.
What is a global gitignore and why use one?

A .gitignore in the repository describes what that project should not track, and belongs in version control. A global ignore file, set with git config --global core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global, covers things specific to you: .DS_Store, editor directories such as .idea/ and .vscode/, and local scratch files. The distinction matters as courtesy: your colleagues on other systems should not have to carry ignore rules for your operating system and editor.
What Git settings should everyone change from the defaults?

Four are worth setting immediately. init.defaultBranch main, so new repositories match what hosting platforms expect. pull.rebase true, which stops a plain git pull littering history with merge commits. fetch.prune true, so branches deleted upstream disappear from your local list. And core.editor set to something you can exit, which spares you meeting Vim unexpectedly. Adding rerere.enabled true pays for itself the first time you rebase through the same conflict twice.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a Git submodule?

A submodule is a reference from one repository to a specific commit of another. The parent repository records the child's URL in .gitmodules and the exact commit in its tree, not the files themselves. That pinning is the feature: the parent always checks out a known version of the dependency rather than whatever the other repository's main happens to be. It is also the source of most confusion, because the submodule is a separate repository with its own history, branches and remote.
Why is my submodule directory empty after cloning?

Because a plain git clone records the submodule but does not fetch its contents. Clone with git clone --recurse-submodules <url>, or fix an existing clone with git submodule update --init --recursive. Setting git config --global submodule.recurse true makes clone, pull and checkout handle submodules automatically, which removes an entire category of "it works on my machine" from a team using them.
How do I update a submodule to the latest commit?

Two different operations, easily conflated. git submodule update --init --recursive checks out the commit the parent has pinned. This is what you want after pulling someone else's change. git submodule update --remote fetches the submodule's tracked branch and moves the pin to its newest commit, which is a change to the parent repository and must be committed there. Running the second when you meant the first is how a submodule silently jumps versions.
Why is my submodule in a detached HEAD state?

Because that is by design: the parent pins a commit, not a branch, so the submodule is checked out at that exact commit with no branch attached. Committing there produces work that belongs to no branch. If you intend to make changes, cd into the submodule and git switch main (or the relevant branch) first, then commit and push in the submodule, and only afterwards commit the new pin in the parent.
What is the difference between Git submodules and subtrees?

Submodules keep the dependency as a separate repository and store only a pointer, which keeps histories clean and requires every contributor to understand submodule commands. Subtrees copy the dependency's files into the parent repository, so a normal clone gets everything and no extra commands are needed, at the cost of merging the other project's history into yours and a fiddlier update path. Subtree is kinder to contributors; submodule is stricter about separation.
Should I use submodules at all?

Only when you genuinely need to pin another repository at a known commit and cannot use a package manager. A published package, npm, PyPI, Go modules, a Terraform module registry, solves the same problem with far better tooling, versioning and caching. Submodules earn their place for vendored forks, shared configuration repositories, and monorepo-adjacent setups where no packaging exists. If a package manager can express the dependency, use it instead.

sections.title: Why Good Commit Messages Matter
paragraphs: A commit message is part of your project's long-term memory. It explains why a change exists and helps later readers understand what happened without opening every file diff first.

A weak message like fix stuff quickly becomes useless. A stronger message like fix(auth): handle expired refresh tokens gives useful context immediately.
Tip: Write commit messages for the person reading them months later, not just for the moment you type them.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What makes a good Git commit message?

A short imperative summary under about 50 characters, "Fix login redirect loop", not "Fixed" or "Fixes", then a blank line, then a body explaining why the change was needed if it is not obvious. The summary appears in git log --oneline, on pull requests and in git blame, so it has to stand alone. The body is where the value is: the diff already shows what changed, and only the message can record the reasoning, the alternative you rejected, or the ticket that prompted it.
Why should commit messages use the imperative mood?

Because Git itself does. Its generated messages read "Merge branch 'main'" and "Revert 'Add caching'", so an imperative summary sits consistently alongside them. The practical test is that the message should complete the sentence "If applied, this commit will…", "Add rate limiting" reads correctly, "Added rate limiting" does not. It is a convention rather than a rule, and its real benefit is consistency: a log where every line is phrased the same way is far quicker to scan.
What are Conventional Commits and do I need them?

A format that prefixes the summary with a type and optional scope: feat(auth): add password reset, fix: handle empty cart, chore(deps): bump axios. The point is machine readability. Tooling can derive a changelog and the next semantic version from the log without anyone maintaining either by hand. You need them if you want automated releases or generated changelogs. If you do not, the discipline still helps, but plain clear messages are perfectly adequate.
How do Conventional Commits map to semantic versioning?

fix: produces a patch bump, feat: a minor bump, and a breaking change a major bump. A breaking change is marked either with ! after the type, feat!: drop Node 18 support, or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer in the body. Tools such as semantic-release read the commits since the last tag, work out the highest bump implied, then tag the release and write the changelog. That is why the format is strict: the version number is derived from it.
How do I change a commit message I already pushed?

git commit --amend rewrites the most recent message, but amending changes the commit hash, so a pushed commit then needs git push --force-with-lease. That is acceptable on your own feature branch and not on a shared one, where everyone who pulled is left on a commit that no longer exists. For older commits, git rebase -i HEAD~n and marking them reword does the same job with the same caveat. On main, the honest answer is to leave it.
How do I enforce commit message rules across a team?

Use commitlint with a commit-msg hook, installed through Husky so the hook lives in the repository and arrives with a clone. Raw .git/hooks files are not version-controlled and so never reach anyone else. That rejects a badly formatted message before the commit is created. Back it up with a server-side check in CI, since local hooks can be skipped with --no-verify; a pull request check that validates the commits is what actually makes the convention stick.
